title: Βωταλὶς καὶ νυκτερίς
part: The Songbird and the Bat (Chambry 75 · Perry 48)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 75 (= Perry 48). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Βωταλὶς ἀπό τινος θυρίδος κρεμαμένη νυκτὸς ᾖδε.
sentences.tr: Bōtalis apo tinos thyridos kremamenē nyktos ēide.
sentences.l: A songbird, hanging from a window, sang by night.
sentences.n: βωταλίς is a rare bird-name; the old lexicons can do no better than 'some small bird', and the identification is honestly a guess — the fable only needs a bird that sings. The bird 'hangs' because its cage does; the cage is left unsaid. νυκτός is the genitive of time within which, 'in the course of the night', matched later by ἡμέρας, 'by day'.

sentences.t: Νυκτερὶς δὲ ἐξήκουσε αὐτῆς τὴν φωνὴν καὶ προσελθοῦσα ἐπυνθάνετο ἀπ’ αὐτῆς τὴν αἰτίαν δι’ ἣν ἡμέρας μὲν ἡσυχάζει, νύκτωρ δὲ ᾄδει.
sentences.tr: Nykteris de exēkouse autēs tēn phōnēn kai proselthousa epynthaneto ap’ autēs tēn aitian di’ hēn hēmeras men hēsychazei, nyktōr de āidei.
sentences.l: And a bat heard her voice from afar and, having come up, asked of her the reason for which by day she keeps quiet, but by night sings.
sentences.i: A bat heard her voice from a distance, came up, and asked her the reason why she was silent by day and sang by night.
sentences.n: δι’ ἥν opens a relative clause inside the reported question, and Greek keeps the tense the bat actually used: ἡσυχάζει and ᾄδει stay present ('why do you keep quiet… and sing?') where English slips them into the past. ἡμέρας (genitive) and νύκτωρ (an adverb) are two different ways of saying when — Greek does not insist on matching them.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ λεγούσης ὡς οὐ μάτην τοῦτο πράττει· ἡμέρας γάρ ποτε ᾄδουσα συνελήφθη, διὸ ἀπ’ ἐκείνου ἐσωφρονίσθη, ἡ νυκτερὶς εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ οὐ νῦν σε δεῖ φυλάττεσθαι, ὅτε οὐδὲν ὄφελός ἐστι, τότε δὲ πρὶν ἢ συλληφθῆναι. »
sentences.tr: Tēs de legousēs hōs ou matēn touto prattei· hēmeras gar pote āidousa synelēphthē, dio ap’ ekeinou esōphronisthē, hē nykteris eipen· « All’ ou nyn se dei phylattesthai, hote ouden ophelos esti, tote de prin ē syllēphthēnai. »
sentences.l: And she saying that she does this not without reason — for once, singing by day, she was caught, and so from that time she was brought to her senses — the bat said: « But it is not now that you must be on your guard, when there is no use in it, but then, before being caught. »
sentences.i: When she answered that she did not do it for nothing — once, singing by day, she had been caught, and had learnt better ever since — the bat said: « But now is not the time to be careful, when it is no use at all; then was the time, before you were caught. »
sentences.n: A genitive absolute, τῆς δὲ λεγούσης, carries the bird's whole answer before the main clause arrives. ὡς after a verb of saying introduces the report, exactly like ὅτι. ἐσωφρονίσθη is the aorist passive of σωφρονίζω, 'she was made prudent' — Greek makes learning a lesson something done to you. πρὶν ἤ with the infinitive, 'before being caught', leaves the person unexpressed.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀτυχήμασι μετάνοια ἀνωφελὴς καθέστηκεν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti epi tois atychēmasi metanoia anōphelēs kathestēken.
sentences.l: The story shows that in the case of misfortunes regret has come to be useless.
sentences.i: The story shows that once the harm is done, second thoughts are of no use.
sentences.n: καθέστηκεν is the perfect of καθίστημι used intransitively: 'has come to be, is and stays' — a settled state, not an event. μετάνοια is literally an after-thought, a change of mind; the heavy religious sense of 'repentance' belongs to later Greek, and here it is simply regretting too late.
